title: A model of unconventional monetary policy
summary_en: Quantitative easing and central-bank balance-sheet expansion looked like emergency-only tools in 2008–9. Gertler and Karádi build a dynamic stochastic general-equilibrium model with financial intermediaries facing balance-sheet constraints and show that, when private credit markets are impaired, central-bank credit-policy interventions (purchasing assets, lending against collateral) can substantially offset the resulting contraction in output and inflation. The paper provided the first widely-cited DSGE microfoundation for unconventional monetary policy and helped reframe QE as a standard counter-cyclical instrument.
data_used: Theoretical / quantitative paper. No primary dataset; the model is calibrated to standard US macroeconomic moments and used to simulate counter-factual policy experiments around the 2008 crisis.
policy_relevance: Directly relevant for the MNB and ECB-watching Hungarian analysts when evaluating unconventional monetary-policy programmes (MNB Funding for Growth, FX swap-line operations, asset-purchase schemes): the framework is the workhorse for assessing whether QE-style interventions are quantitatively meaningful in a small open economy. Practical lesson: the size of the gain depends on how binding intermediaries' balance-sheet constraints are — a setting parameter that needs to be calibrated to Hungary specifically.
